passage:
Supervisor's note, Wednesday
The July rain flooded Tenzin's ground-floor flat on Monday night. He came in on Tuesday in borrowed clothes, having lost his documents and his laptop. At lunch someone muttered that he should have known better than to rent near the nala.
Nirmala put her plate down. "He rented what he could afford. Rain doesn't check who deserves it." Then she moved to practical things: she collected spare clothes from the team, helped him list which documents to apply for again, and offered her sofa for the week.
This morning she came to me with a written request: a short emergency-leave rule for staff hit by floods, so the next person doesn't have to beg for days off. I've forwarded it to HR with my support.
— Kavita, supervisor

qa.q: What did Tenzin lose in the flood?
qa.a: He lost his documents and his laptop.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's reply at lunch show about what she believes?
qa.a: It shows she feels sympathy for Tenzin rather than blame; she believes he simply rented what he could afford and the rain hit him by chance.

qa.q: Which of Nirmala's choices reaches beyond Tenzin, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Her written request for an emergency-leave rule turns one act of kindness into fairness for the whole team, so the next person hit by a flood needn't beg.

qa.q: How might Tenzin, in borrowed clothes, have felt hearing the lunch comment and then Nirmala's reply?
qa.a: The comment probably stung on top of losing so much, and Nirmala's reply may have made him feel defended rather than judged.

grounding: A supervisor sees a young woman reject blame for a flooded colleague, help practically, and push for a fair leave rule.

passage:
Thursday, 11 pm
Sachin was one of the forty let go today. Forty, in one email. He's the person who stayed late fixing other people's bugs.
By lunch the whispers had started: "He must have been on some list for a reason." I felt it too, for a second, that tidy thought: if he did something wrong, I'm safe. Then I heard Amma's voice in my head: "Beti, don't ask why; ask what he needs."
So I asked. He needed his old project files, a reference, and someone to sit with at the tea stall while he called home. I did all three.
Tonight I started a shared sheet of openings for everyone who was let go, not just my friends. Eleven names already.
Bad things land on good people. The least I can do is not add blame.
— Chandrika

qa.q: How many people were let go in the email?
qa.a: Forty were let go, in one email.

qa.q: Why did the 'tidy thought' tempt Chandrika for a second?
qa.a: If Sachin did something wrong, then Chandrika could feel safe from the same email; the thought protects her more than it explains anything.

qa.q: What choice did Chandrika make after catching that thought, and how did it help?
qa.a: She asked Sachin what he needed instead of why it happened, then got him the files, a reference and company at the tea stall.

qa.q: How might the other people who were let go see Chandrika's shared sheet?
qa.a: They may feel less alone and less judged, since the sheet treats everyone who lost a job as deserving help, not just her friends.

grounding: A young woman resists blaming a laid-off colleague, supports him practically and opens help fairly to all.

passage:
(Trisha texts her friend Ojas the evening after his scooter accident.)
Trisha: how's the arm? 🤍
Ojas: plastered. and I missed the licensing exam. two years of prep
Ojas: my chachi says it's karma. maybe I did something
Trisha: a car jumped a red light. that's not karma, that's a car
Trisha: you didn't earn this. it just happened to you
Ojas: feels like everyone thinks I did
Trisha: not me. want me to bring dinner tomorrow and sit with you?
Ojas: yes pls 🙏
Trisha: also I checked, the exam board has a medical re-sit form. I'll help you fill it
Trisha: and I'm emailing them to put that form on the main page. half the people who need it don't even know it exists
Ojas: you're kind of amazing

qa.q: Which exam did Ojas miss?
qa.a: Ojas missed the licensing exam.

qa.q: What is Ojas worried about when he writes 'maybe I did something'?
qa.a: After his chachi's karma comment, Ojas worries the accident is a punishment, which adds shame to the pain of losing two years of prep.

qa.q: Which of Trisha's choices goes beyond comforting Ojas, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Emailing the exam board to put the re-sit form on the main page helps everyone who needs it, not only Ojas.

qa.q: How might Ojas's chachi see the accident, and what would change if she saw it as Trisha does?
qa.a: The chachi seems to look for a hidden reason behind it; if she saw it as plain bad luck, she might offer help instead of making Ojas feel guilty.

grounding: A young woman rejects karma talk after a friend's accident, supports him and pushes for a clearer re-sit rule.

passage:
The hailstorm lasted twenty minutes and flattened Akash's whole wheat field outside the village near Bhopal. Next morning, at the tea stall, someone said, "His father fought with the temple committee. What goes around comes around." Others nodded.
Aparna, twenty-six, the agriculture extension worker, put down her glass. "The hail fell on his field and on the Rathores' field too. Did they fight with anyone?" Nobody answered.
She walked to Akash's house. He was sitting in the yard, not speaking. She didn't say it was destiny or a lesson. She said, "This was bad luck, and it's heavy. I'm here." She sat with him for an hour, then helped him photograph the damage and fill the relief form at the block office.
Back at the office, she pushed for the hailstorm survey to cover every farm in the area, not just the big ones.

qa.q: How long did the hailstorm last?
qa.a: The hailstorm lasted twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Aparna seem to feel when she heard the tea-stall talk?
qa.a: Aparna seemed troubled and unwilling to accept the blame, which is why she put down her glass and pointed out that the hail also fell on the Rathores' field.

qa.q: What did Aparna do for Akash, and what did she do for fairness more widely?
qa.a: She sat with him and helped him photograph the damage and fill the relief form, then pushed for the survey to cover every farm, not just the big ones.

qa.q: How might Akash have experienced Aparna's visit?
qa.a: Akash, sitting silently in the yard, may have felt less alone and less judged when she called it bad luck instead of a punishment.

grounding: It shows a young worker accepting that bad things happen to good people, supporting the farmer, and working for a fairer survey.

passage:
Zeynep's little café on a side street in Lyon closed in March. The landlord sold the building and the new owner doubled the rent overnight. Zeynep had run it for four years, and every morning she remembered her regulars' orders.
At the neighbourhood meeting, one man said, "She should have seen it coming. Bad planning." Another said, "Those things don't happen to people who are careful."
Amara, twenty-five, who lived above the bakery, felt her jaw tighten. She stood up. "Zeynep was careful. She paid every bill on time. Sometimes it's just bad luck, and a bad system."
After the meeting she went to Zeynep's flat with soup and sat on the sofa with her, mostly listening.
The next week Amara started a petition asking the council for longer notice before rent increases on small shops. Zeynep signed it first, her hand shaking a little.

qa.q: How many years had Zeynep run the café?
qa.a: Zeynep had run it for four years.

qa.q: What does Amara's tightening jaw suggest she felt at the meeting?
qa.a: It suggests she felt angry and protective, disagreeing strongly with the idea that Zeynep caused her own misfortune.

qa.q: What did Amara do both to support Zeynep and to work for fairness?
qa.a: She visited with soup and mostly listened, and then started a petition asking for longer notice before rent increases on small shops.

qa.q: How might Zeynep feel hearing Amara defend her at the meeting?
qa.a: Zeynep would likely feel less alone and less ashamed, knowing someone saw her as careful and the loss as bad luck rather than a failure.

grounding: It shows a young woman accepting that bad things happen to good people, supporting a neighbour and working for a fairer rule.
